statements.text: Congress is grappling with technology. Our country's grappling with technology. And we're doing our best to try to figure out a regulatory environment that fosters innovation and allows economic growth, while managing the potential adverse impacts that technology can have. [...] But I do want to talk about AI's potential impact on our work force, particularly how tech can be leveraged to further individual efficiency rather than possibly displace workers.
statements.context: US Representative William Timmons (R-SC) questioning expert witnesses at a congressional hearing titled 'Advances in AI: Are We Ready for a Tech Revolution?'

statements.text: And I think as it relates to weaponizing it, one of the benefits is the speed at which it can act. And if you have a drone swarm that is AI enabled, I mean, how do you incorporate the human component? Because the whole benefit of using AI in that scenario would be the speed at which it is able to act.
statements.context: House hearing on federal agency use of artificial intelligence, where a member questions witnesses about military applications of AI.

statements.text: So, I mean, we could easily say if you create this, there is a civil penalty that is available, and that if you do this, there is a criminal penalty, just like states have done with revenge porn.
statements.context: Hearing titled 'Advances in Deepfake Technology' featuring an exchange between Representative Timmons and a witness.

statements.text: Theoretically, we could mandate certain websites to use AI to identify deepfakes and automatically delete them if they are deemed pornographic. Theoretically.
statements.context: US lawmaker speaking at a hearing or discussion on 'Advances in Deepfake Technology'.

statements.text: How can Congress create a regulatory framework that protects against potential harm associated with AI while not impeding the development and implementation of all the benefits that AI has to offer? [...] I am concerned that businesses will just relocate abroad if our regulatory framework becomes overly complex or burdensome.
statements.context: Member of Congress questions expert witnesses at a hearing on White House AI policy.

statements.text: As we stand on the precipice of a technological revolution driven by AI, it is imperative that our regulatory frameworks are not only sufficient to manage risk and foster innovation in this emerging technology, but are also harmonized across all of government. [...] However, with great power comes great responsibility. As we witness the rapid advancements in AI technology, it becomes increasingly clear that a patchwork of disjointed regulations is not sufficient to address the complex challenges and ethical considerations that AI presents.
statements.context: Speaking at a congressional hearing on White House AI policy, the lawmaker questions a witness about the NIST AI Risk Management Framework after noting the dangers of AI-enabled weaponry.

statements.text: As businesses try to compete in the free market, they're inevitably going to try to cut costs and replace work force with technology. What--how are we going to manage that challenge?
statements.venue: House Oversight subcommittee hearing 'Advances in AI: Are We Ready for a Tech Revolution?'

statements.text: If you use ChatGPT and you ask a question, and then you say, answer that question if you are in Saudi Arabia or if you are in Yemen, it is actually quite different.
statements.context: House lawmaker questioning a witness during a hearing on building an AI-ready workforce.

statements.text: But again, Congress does need to act, to be fair, so maybe we should get our act together and address this in a way that can facilitate innovation and keep the United States on the forefront of being the best economy in the world.
statements.venue: House Oversight hearing 'White House Overreach on AI'

statements.text: And I am reading some of this, and, you know, it requires a quantity of computing power greater than 10 to the integer. I do not think the American people have any idea what that means, so with all due respect, the American people did not write this. Mr. Thierer, do you have any understanding of how this would be enforced in regard to noncompliance? I mean, would the CEO or would board members go to jail? Like, how would that work?
statements.context: House hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' where Congressman Timmons questions a witness about the enforceability of a Biden-era AI executive order provision.

statements.text: That said, we do need to address AI, and just because Congress is unable to address AI as quickly as we should does not give the President the right to legislate for us.
statements.context: House committee hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' with a member arguing that executive action on AI is improper.

While there are many challenges involved in legislating and establishing clear rules of the road for artificial intelligence, there are also powerful opportunities. [...] Artificial intelligence has the potential to equip financial institutions with advanced tools to better serve their clients, improve efficiency, and reduce risk.
statements.context: US congressional hearing titled 'Unlocking the Next Generation of AI in the U.S. Financial System for Consumers, Businesses, and Competitiveness,' where a lawmaker questions a witness.

statements.text: I am increasingly concerned about the growing number of conflicting State laws related to AI. [...] Without a unified approach, we risk slowing progress and creating barriers that disadvantage both American businesses and the people they serve.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Timmons at a House Financial Services Subcommittee hearing on AI in the U.S. financial system.

statements.text: I am going to turn that a little bit around and say, while this is going to be difficult for financial services companies to comply and to work across State lines, let us talk about the AI companies that are trying to create these products. [...] the Chinese are ahead of us or close to being ahead of us, and the businesses that they have that are focused on this do not have this burden. Would you say that is an equally difficult challenge?
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI in the U.S. financial system, questioning a witness about regulatory burdens and international competitiveness.

statements.text: I think everyone agrees that we need to have a Federal standard that preempts everything and leads in the global economy, and we are not learning from past mistakes. [...] So not only do we need to lead here in Congress on AI, but we also need to get with the program and address the patchwork framework that is costing incredible amounts of money for compliance for businesses.
statements.context: Speaking at a Financial Services Committee hearing on AI innovation, the lawmaker urges a unified federal AI framework to avoid state-level regulatory fragmentation.

statements.text: A follow up question. Many State proposals include different documentation and testing requirements for similar artificial intelligence systems. From an operational point of view, how difficult is it for a cloud provider or a financial institution to adjust model governance and controls to comply with several conflicting regimes?
statements.context: Asked during a panel or hearing on AI innovation in financial services.

statements.text: If the United States is going to remain a global leader in innovation, we must adopt clear and harmonized rules that support technological progress while also protecting consumers and preserving market integrity. Industry leaders are increasingly concerned about the growing patchwork of state laws related to artificial intelligence.
statements.venue: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI in financial services

statements.text: Without a unified federal framework that replaces duplicative and contradictory state rules, we risk higher compliance costs, slower innovation, and weaker protection for consumers.
statements.venue: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI in financial services

statements.text: AI is the way of the future, and America must continue to develop and advance it if we want to remain competitive in the global arena. President Trump has led the way in growing our AI capabilities and it is crucial for Congress to follow his lead to keep our economy and national security strong.
statements.venue: House Oversight press release (joint statement of Subcommittee Chairmen Burlison and Timmons)

statements.text: The solution is not us slowing down emerging technology [...] That’s just going to push all of the innovation overseas. We cannot do that; we have to lead.
